analysis.one_liner: Caps what families pay for phone calls to relatives in prison and bans prison commissions from phone carriers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill told the Federal Communications Commission to set caps on the per-minute and per-call charges that prison phone companies bill to families of incarcerated people. It would also require carriers to offer both collect calling and debit accounts, ban the commissions carriers paid to prisons for exclusive contracts, and require prisons to allow more than one phone provider so callers had a choice. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of incarcerated people — typically low-income households who pay the phone bills, since prisoners can only place calls and the recipient is billed. The bill's own findings describe per-minute rates reaching $1 and connection fees of $3.95 per call, with commissions to prisons making up half or more of the total charge.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to consider maximum uniform per-minute and per-call rates for interstate inmate calls, so families pay a price closer to an ordinary long-distance rate.

Prohibits the commissions that phone carriers pay to prison administrators for the exclusive right to serve a facility — commissions the bill found could account for 50 percent or more of the total charges.

Requires carriers to offer both collect calling and debit account services and requires facilities to allow more than one provider, so callers could pick the cheapest option instead of being locked into a single monopoly carrier.
States as a congressional finding that keeping regular family contact reduces recidivism and helps people reintegrate after release, and that excessive rates burden and can prevent that contact.

analysis.who_pays: Inmate telephone carriers lose monopoly profits and commission payments, and state and local corrections departments lose the commission revenue they collected on inmate call bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone carriers and corrections agencies

drawbacks.text: Banning commissions would cut off revenue that corrections agencies collect on inmate calls, which some agencies use to fund inmate programs and facility costs — a real cost the bill does not provide a replacement for.

The bill only directs the FCC to 'consider' types of regulation, including caps; it guarantees a rulemaking process, not a guaranteed rate cap, and carriers could argue that any cap must still cover the cost of security screening and specialized service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is strong and concrete: families, many of them low-income, were paying among the highest phone rates in the country, largely because of monopoly contracts and commissions that had nothing to do with the cost of the call. The costs fall on carriers' margins and on prison agencies' commission revenue; the concern that commissions fund inmate programs is legitimate but could be addressed by funding programs directly rather than taxing families' phone calls. On the merits this is a modest, well-targeted consumer bill whose main weakness was that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on February 23, 2009 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Communications Subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush (D-IL) introduced the Family Telephone Connection Protection Act of 2009 on February 23, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and, one day later, to its Subcommittee on Communications, Technology, and the Internet.
The bill had a single cosponsor, a House Democrat, and no further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

The bill's findings described inmate-call rates reaching $1 per minute plus $3.95 connection fees, driven by single-carrier monopoly contracts and commissions to prison administrators that reached 50 percent or more of the charges.

The bill would have required the FCC to run a rulemaking within one year on capping rates, banning commissions, requiring collect and debit payment options, and allowing multiple carriers per facility, and to preempt inconsistent state rules.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Inmate telephone carriers kept their exclusive facility contracts and the state and local corrections agencies kept collecting commissions on the calls, while low-income families continued paying some of the highest phone rates in the country. The practical relief this bill sought did not happen through it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone carriers and state corrections agencies

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 23, 2009 and wrote findings on monopoly rates and prison commissions.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Communications, Technology, and the Internet
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on February 24, 2009.

against.name: Inmate telephone service providers
against.what_they_did: Had an economic stake in keeping exclusive facility contracts and commissions; the industry fought rate regulation and commission bans for years in regulatory and court proceedings around this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split was recorded; the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats and the bill died under a Democratic House majority, meaning the opposition that mattered was inaction, not a party-bloc vote.

industries.note: The bill would cap their per-minute and per-call charges, ban the commissions they pay prisons for exclusive contracts, and force them to accept competing providers and debit-payment options. Their revenue depended on monopoly contracts with facilities and rates far above ordinary long-distance prices, paid by families who had no alternative.

The bill would end the commissions these agencies collected from phone carriers based on inmate call revenue, and require them to allow more than one carrier per facility. Agencies often used this revenue for inmate programs, though it was raised from prisoners' families.
